title: Caltech Chip Redirects Light in 74 Quadrillionths of a Second
summary:
In 74 quadrillionths of a second, light can barely cross the width of a human hair. That's also how fast a new Caltech chip can redirect a beam of light.

Researchers have developed a device that uses one beam of light to steer another in just 74 femtoseconds — a femtosecond being a quadrillionth of a second. Light can carry huge amounts of information, which is why photonic technologies (systems that use light instead of electricity) are being explored for faster communications, more powerful computing, and highly sensitive sensors.

The challenge is control. Most existing technologies steer light by changing a material's electronic properties — like the liquid-crystal panels in projectors. Electrons get pushed into higher energy states, then relax back down, releasing energy. That relaxation takes time, creating a bottleneck that usually limits light modulation to nanosecond or picosecond timescales.

Caltech's team removed the electrical signal entirely. They used a powerful "pump" beam with a carefully designed pattern to temporarily alter a material's optical behavior. A weaker "probe" beam then passed through and changed direction according to that pattern. The system relies on the optical Kerr effect: when intense light passes through a material, it briefly changes the material's refractive index — how much light slows and bends inside it. Crucially, electrons aren't pushed into long-lasting excited states, so the change appears and vanishes almost as fast as the light pulse itself.

On its own the Kerr effect is too weak to be useful. So the researchers built a meta-surface — an ultrathin, nanoengineered sheet — from amorphous silicon, covered with nanoscale pillars smaller than the pump light's wavelength. These pillars keep light circulating inside slightly longer, amplifying the effect. "Using optical meta-surfaces, we can up the interaction strength," says Harry Atwater of Caltech.

The result: light steered by angles up to 13 degrees in 74 femtoseconds. The speed limit comes from the laser pulses, not the material — meaning faster lasers could push it further.

Faster light steering could transform communications, computing, and sensing. Not bad for something thinner than a wavelength of light.
why_it_matters: Almost every fast technology a teenager relies on — streaming video, cloud computing, data centres — is limited by how quickly signals can be switched, and this result shows the bottleneck can be bypassed by using light's own behaviour instead of electronics, pointing toward computers and networks that move data at entirely different speeds.

background_read: Caltech (the California Institute of Technology, a research university in Pasadena, California) runs some of the world's leading programs in optics and materials science, and Harry Atwater, quoted in the article, leads photonics research there.

Light is the fastest thing in the universe and carries information very efficiently, which is why fibre-optic cables — thin strands of glass that guide light over long distances — form the backbone of the global internet. In those networks light has to be switched and steered constantly, and the devices that do this job are a known bottleneck: most of them work by nudging electrons inside a material, and electrons take time to settle back down.

The optical Kerr effect is named after John Kerr, a Scottish physicist who described it in the 1800s, and it is the reason a powerful laser beam can change how a material bends light. The effect is usually far too weak to be useful on its own, which is where meta-surfaces come in: flat, nanoengineered sheets dotted with structures smaller than the wavelength of the light, letting engineers manipulate light in ways natural materials cannot.
Results like this one matter beyond the lab, because faster light steering would speed up data centres, sensors and eventually computers that calculate with light rather than electrons.

perspectives.description: The device sidesteps the electron-relaxation bottleneck completely, steering light faster than most existing modulation schemes can manage. If it holds up, it could feed into communications, computing and sensing, all areas where photonics already outperforms electronics on speed.

The demonstration needs a powerful pump laser, steers light by only 13 degrees and works on a tiny meta-surface, so nothing here is close to a product. Power consumption, cost, durability and whether the trick scales to chip-sized manufacturing are all unresolved questions.

This fits a recurring pattern in photonics research: when electronics impose a limit, engineers replace the electrical signal with a purely optical one. Meta-surfaces have become a standard way of amplifying effects that are otherwise too weak, so the innovation is as much about materials engineering as about physics.

Since the speed limit comes from the laser pulses rather than the material itself, the obvious next experiments use faster lasers and different meta-surface designs. The longer-term question is integration: whether such devices can be built with the same silicon-style processes used for ordinary chips, at a cost that makes sense.
